questions.question: What must a topic sentence do for a paragraph, and where can it sit?
questions.solution: It states the paragraph's single controlling idea — everything after must support it, and anything unrelated belongs in another paragraph. It usually opens the paragraph but can sit mid-paragraph (after a hook) or at the end as a conclusion; the test is whether it governs the rest. One paragraph = one idea.

questions.question: A paragraph uses 'however, therefore, moreover' correctly but still reads as disconnected. What is missing — cohesion or coherence?
questions.solution: It has COHESION (linking devices) but lacks COHERENCE (logical order of ideas). Coherence is the underlying plan: each sentence advances the controlling idea in a sensible sequence (general → specific, chronological, cause → effect). Connectives cannot rescue a disordered argument — fix the order first, then link.

questions.concept: Essay structure — the job of each part
questions.question: State what the introduction, body and conclusion of an essay must each accomplish — no more, no less.
questions.solution: Introduction: engage, give necessary context, and state the THESIS (the essay's claim). Body: develop the thesis point by point, one paragraph per point, each with evidence. Conclusion: restate the thesis in light of the evidence and close with significance — no NEW arguments. Introductions that argue and conclusions that introduce are the two classic structural errors.

questions.question: What must a formal letter (e.g. to an editor) contain that an informal letter to a friend must not?
questions.solution: Sender's address and date, the recipient's designation and address, a formal salutation (Dear Sir/Madam), a subject line stating the purpose, formal register throughout, and a formal close (Yours faithfully/sincerely) with full name. Content is purpose-driven: state the issue, the facts, and the action requested. Informal letters may drop all of these for a conversational tone.

questions.question: Why does a report avoid opinions and first-person narration, and what structure does it follow?
questions.solution: A report communicates verified information to a reader who needs to ACT on it — so it uses the passive/impersonal voice, past tense, and only verifiable facts with figures. Structure: headline/title, by-line, lead paragraph answering what/when/where/who, body expanding the details, and a factual conclusion. Opinion belongs in an article or editorial, not a report.

questions.concept: Article vs speech — the audience shift
questions.question: The same topic (plastic pollution) is set as an article and as a speech. What must change between the two drafts?
questions.solution: Article: written for a silent reader — headline, byline, formal-informative tone, data and arguments, no direct address. Speech: delivered aloud — a greeting to the audience, direct address ('my friends'), rhetorical questions, repetition and a strong call to action, simpler sentence rhythm for the ear. The audience's mode of reception (eye vs ear) drives every difference.

questions.question: Why do note-making conventions ban full sentences and demand abbreviations, headings and indentation?
questions.solution: Notes are for the note-maker's later retrieval, not for another reader: keywords (not sentences) compress information, headings/indentation expose the HIERARCHY of ideas (main point → support → example), and abbreviations save time. The test of good notes is whether you can reconstruct the passage from them alone — structure, not prose, is what carries the meaning.

questions.question: Why should a CV for a programming internship omit the applicant's primary-school prizes?
questions.solution: A CV is a RELEVANCE-filtered argument that you fit the specific role: every line should support employability for THAT post. Old, irrelevant items dilute the strong recent ones and signal poor judgement about what matters. Order by recency and relevance, quantify achievements, and keep it to the length the employer will actually read.
